Purpose — This platform consolidates the full body of doctoral research on assessing the public’s Knowledge, Attitude, and Perception (KAP) toward antimicrobial resistance (AMR). 🌍 Research Context, Rationale & Significance

Antimicrobial Resistance — A Global Health Crisis

Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is recognised by the World Health Organization as one of the top ten global public-health threats facing humanity. Bacterial AMR was associated with an estimated 4.95 million deaths and directly attributable to 1.27 million deaths worldwide in 2019, with projections of up to 10 million annual deaths by 2050 under current trajectories.

A principal, modifiable driver of resistance is inappropriate antibiotic use by the general public — self-medication, non-prescription purchase, premature discontinuation of courses, and the sharing or reuse of leftover antibiotics. These behaviours are especially prevalent in settings where antibiotics are accessible without prescription, making the public a decisive front in AMR containment.

Why KAP Assessment Is Critical & Study Objectives

Knowledge, Attitude and Perception (KAP) jointly determine antibiotic-related behaviour. Valid measurement of these constructs is a prerequisite for designing, targeting and evaluating any public-education intervention. This doctoral research therefore pursues three objectives:

  1. Construct and validate a culturally-adapted bilingual KAP instrument for the Iranian adult public;
  2. Design and refine an evidence-based serious game (“Health City / ”) grounded in behaviour-change theory;
  3. Measure KAP change through a two-arm randomised controlled trial (RCT).

Significance: the study delivers a reusable, psychometrically validated instrument and a theory-driven intervention model directly relevant to Iran’s national AMR action plan and transferable to comparable settings.

Platform Purpose & Key Milestones Achieved

This bilingual platform is the central knowledge hub of the PhD workflow, consolidating every artefact — systematic-review metrics, the validated instrument, game-design documents, methodology and population analysis — into a single, self-contained, reproducible interface for supervision, dissemination and archival.

Key milestones achieved to date:

  • 2,685 articles screened in the systematic review;
  • 1,644-item candidate KAP bank assembled and curated;
  • 50 validated items (25 Knowledge / 15 Attitude / 10 Perception) finalised;
  • 19-member expert panel validation with S-CVI/Ave = 0.966;
  • Game Design Document reviewed (7.2/10) and refined from Scenario v1 → v2.

Purpose — Content Validity quantifies how well each candidate item represents the AMR-KAP construct, using the Content Validity Ratio (CVR, Lawshe 1975) and the Content Validity Index (CVI, Waltz–Bausell) rated by a 19-member expert panel.

🔗 Research pipeline: Instrument-validation phase — the quantitative gate every item must pass before entering the final KAP instrument.🧪 Methodology: Modified-Delphi expert rating; items retained when CVR ≥ 0.49 and I-CVI ≥ 0.79, yielding an excellent S-CVI/Ave = 0.966.

🔬 Content Validity — CVR / CVI Analysis

Content validity of 18 educational items was rated by a 19-member expert panel using the Lawshe (1975) CVR and Waltz–Bausell CVI procedures via a Modified Delphi design. The final S-CVI/Ave reached 0.966, exceeding the 0.90 threshold for excellent content validity.

✅ Items Accepted (CVR ≥ 0.49, CVI ≥ 0.79)

15 of 18 items met both Lawshe critical-CVR and item-level CVI thresholds and entered the final instrument without modification.

🟡 Items Marked for Revision

3 of 18 items required minor wording refinement based on expert qualitative feedback before inclusion.

🔴 Items Rejected

0 of 18 items were rejected — a strong indicator of robust pre-screening at the systematic-review stage.

📈 Scale-Level Content Validity Index

S-CVI/Ave = 0.966 (95% CI 0.94–0.98) — qualifies as 'excellent' per Polit & Beck (2006) benchmarks.

🧮 Validation Framework, Indices & Decision Criteria

Expert Panel Composition & Selection Criteria

Content validity was established by a 19-member multidisciplinary expert panel spanning infectious-disease medicine, clinical pharmacy, medical microbiology, health education & promotion, public health/epidemiology, and instrument-design methodology. Panellists were purposively selected for relevant clinical or research experience and AMR-related publications, following a Modified-Delphi procedure.

Note: the CV/CVR analysis concerns a focused set of 18 educational items — a distinct content-validation exercise from the 50-item KAP instrument, although both share the same expert-rating methodology.

Content Validity Index (CVI) Methodology

The CVI quantifies expert agreement on item relevance. For each item, the Item-level CVI (I-CVI) is the proportion of experts rating the item 3 or 4 on a 4-point relevance scale: I-CVI = (n rating 3–4) / N. At scale level, S-CVI/Ave is the mean of the I-CVIs and S-CVI/UA the proportion of items rated relevant by all experts.

  • I-CVI ≥ 0.79 retained (Lynn 1986, for panels of ≥ 6 experts);
  • S-CVI/Ave ≥ 0.90 = “excellent” content validity (Polit & Beck 2006);
  • Items were additionally rated for clarity and simplicity to inform wording revisions.

The instrument achieved S-CVI/Ave = 0.966 (95% CI 0.94–0.98).

Content Validity Ratio (CVR) — Lawshe’s Method

The CVR (Lawshe 1975) captures item essentiality. Each expert rates an item as Essential, Useful but not essential, or Not necessary; the ratio is computed as:

CVR = (ne − N/2) / (N/2)

where ne = experts marking the item Essential and N = total panellists. CVR ranges from −1 to +1. With a 19-member panel the critical CVR ≈ 0.42 (one-tailed, p = 0.05; Wilson et al. 2012 update of Lawshe’s table); items meeting this threshold demonstrate non-chance agreement on essentiality.

Decision Criteria, Outcomes & References

An item entered the final instrument when it satisfied both CVR ≥ critical value and I-CVI ≥ 0.79. Items failing one criterion but showing promise were revised per qualitative feedback; items failing both were rejected.

Outcomes: 15/18 accepted unchanged · 3/18 revised · 0/18 rejected — reflecting strong upstream screening at the systematic-review stage.

Anchoring literature: Lawshe (1975); Lynn (1986); Davis (1992); Waltz & Bausell (1981); Polit & Beck (2006); Wilson, Pan & Schumsky (2012).

🔬 Selection Pipeline (4 Stages)

Step 1 — Deduplication. Systematic deduplication and content tagging across the harvested literature removed 403 redundant items, leaving 1,241 unique candidates.
Resources: see reproducible_selection_code.py (Stage 1: deduplicate_items()).

Step 2 — Cultural & Methodological Filtering. Cultural-incompatibility screening (Iran-specific pharmacy access, family medication-sharing norms) removed 13 items; methodological-quality screening (validity, scaling, ambiguity) removed an additional 48 items → 1,180 items.
Resources: see reproducible_selection_code.py (Stage 2: cultural_filter(), methodological_filter()).

Step 3 — Evidence-Based Multi-Criteria Weighting. The 1,180-item pool was scored on 5 literature-grounded criteria (CV = 0.30, CR = 0.25, BC = 0.20, RD = 0.15, BL = 0.10). A 22-scenario sensitivity analysis confirmed robustness (mean Jaccard 0.911), classifying every item as core, sensitive, or never_top50, and producing a 275-item longlist.
Resources: see reproducible_selection_code.py (Stage 3: score_and_rank(), run_sensitivity()); expert ratings collected via KAP_Expert_Rating_Form_v13.xlsx.

Step 4 — Cultural & Plain-Language Validation. Cultural-adaptation review (CAF rules) and plain-language rewriting (7th–8th grade readability) in EN and FA, then domain-stratified maximum-coverage sampling selected the final 50 items (K = 25 / A = 15 / P = 10) across Knowledge / Attitude / Perception.
Resources: final instrument KAP_Research_Instrument_v13.xlsx; aggregated metrics and visuals in KAP_Resource.xlsx.

📄 Selection Methodology & Coverage Report

📑 1 — Item Pool & Provenance

The candidate pool comprised 1644 unique KAP items harvested from peer-reviewed AMR Knowledge-Attitude-Perception instruments and validated questionnaires worldwide (WHO multi-country surveys, Eurobarometer, regional public-health studies). After provenance tagging and language normalisation, the pool entered a 4-stage deterministic selection pipeline yielding the final 50-item validated instrument (K = 25 / A = 15 / P = 10) tailored to the Iranian adult public.

📑 2 — Five-Criterion Weighted Selection (Stage 3)

After de-duplication (1,241 items) and cultural/methodological filtering (1,180 items), the 1,180-item shortlist was scored with a literature-grounded multi-criteria model. The five criteria and their baseline weights:

CodeCriterionBaseline WeightAnchoring Literature
CVContent Validity (CVI / CVR / I-CVI)0.30Lynn 1986; Davis 1992; Lawshe 1975
CRCross-Cultural Relevance & Translatability0.25Beaton 2000; TRAPD; Hashemi 2020
BCBehavioural Coverage (KAP construct breadth)0.20Empirical weighting (this study)
RDReadability & Plain Language (7th–8th grade)0.15Flesch-Kincaid; CDC Plain Language
BLBehavioural Specificity / Self-Medication Locus0.10WHO 2015; Sakeena 2018

Each item received a 0-to-1 score on every criterion; the weighted composite score ranked the 1,180 items and produced the 275-item domain-stratified longlist from which the final 50 items were drawn.

📑 3 — Sensitivity Analysis (22 Scenarios)

To verify robustness of the baseline weighting, the criterion weights were systematically perturbed across 22 alternative scenarios (uniform weights, single-criterion dominance, ±0.05 / ±0.10 sweeps, criterion ablation). For every scenario the top-275 longlist was regenerated and compared with the baseline.

  • core (38 items): appeared in every scenario — always-included; locked into the final 50.
  • sensitive (30 items): boundary-sensitive — included in >50% but not all 22 scenarios; resolved by tie-breaking on CV + readability.
  • never_top50 (207 items): appeared in 0 scenarios — robustly excluded from any plausible top-50.
  • Mean Jaccard similarity: 0.911 across all 22 scenarios (range 0.695 – 1.000), indicating very high agreement between baseline and perturbed rankings.

📑 4 — Cultural & Plain-Language Validation (Stage 4)

The 275-item longlist passed a final cultural-adaptation filter (Cultural Adaptation Framework / CAF rules: pharmacy access norms, family-mediated medication sharing, religious-fasting considerations, urban/rural literacy gap). Items were then re-written in 7th–8th grade plain English and Persian, validated against Flesch-Kincaid readability targets and Iranian Plain Language guidance. The 50 final items were selected by domain-stratified maximum-coverage sampling (K = 25, A = 15, P = 10) such that every behavioural sub-construct (sharing, self-medication, course completion, provider trust, etc.) is represented by 1–3 items.

📑 5 — Coverage Summary

  • Knowledge (25 items) spans 13 sub-constructs from leftover-antibiotic storage and viral-illness misuse to mechanism-of-action and resistance consequences.
  • Attitude (15 items) covers 6 sub-constructs: antibiotic demand, sharing, self-medication, adherence, provider trust, social norms.
  • Perception (10 items) covers 6 sub-constructs: sharing/reuse, provider role, social norms, barriers, demand, self-efficacy.
  • Bilingual deployment: EN-LTR and FA-RTL print-ready instruments are downloadable above; the canonical research instrument is provided as a 6-sheet XLSX.

📝 6 — Expert Review & Methodology Report

The initial 50-item questionnaire, selected through the four-stage pipeline described above, was submitted to two subject-matter experts for independent review. Based on their feedback, 7 items were revised to improve clarity, cultural appropriateness, and terminological consistency for the Iranian general public:

  • K01: Revised for clearer causal framing — emphasising that bacterial resistance makes infection treatment more difficult.
  • K02: Terminology changed from "AMR / antimicrobials" to "antibiotic resistance / antibiotics" for plain-language accessibility.
  • K07: Converted from interrogative to declarative format for consistency with the instrument's statement-based design.
  • K09: Disease examples updated to culturally familiar terms (throat infection, lung infection, wound infection) replacing less common references (typhoid).
  • K22: Drug name changed from "paracetamol" to "acetaminophen" (استامینوفن) to match Iranian pharmacological convention; question format changed to declarative.
  • A02: Rewritten in first-person with a concrete side-effect example (diarrhoea) replacing the generic "adverse side effects" phrasing; terminology changed from "antimicrobials" to "antibiotics".
  • P09: Terminology updated from "antimicrobial resistance" to "antibiotic resistance" (مقاومت آنتی‌بیوتیکی) for consistency across the instrument.

Following these expert-informed revisions, the finalised 50-item questionnaire will be submitted to a specialised expert panel for formal content-validity assessment using the Content Validity Index (CVI) and Content Validity Ratio (CVR) methodology, as described in the Validation Framework section above.

📝Go to Expert Content Validation Form↗

🧪 Item-Selection Pipeline & Instrument Architecture

The Four-Stage Selection Funnel (1,644 → 50)

The 50 final items were distilled from a large candidate bank through a fully documented, deterministic and reproducible pipeline:

StageProcessItems remaining
Step 1 — DeduplicationSystematic deduplication and content tagging removed 403 redundant items from the harvested literature (1,644 → 1,241).1,241
Step 2 — Cultural & Methodological FilteringCultural-incompatibility screening removed 13 items and methodological-quality screening removed 48 items (1,241 → 1,180).1,180
Step 3 — Evidence-Based Multi-Criteria WeightingFive literature-grounded criteria (CV = 0.30, CR = 0.25, BC = 0.20, RD = 0.15, BL = 0.10) with a 22-scenario sensitivity analysis (mean Jaccard 0.911) rank items into a domain-stratified longlist (1,180 → 275).275
Step 4 — Cultural & Plain-Language ValidationCultural-adaptation review (CAF rules) and plain-language rewriting (7th–8th grade readability), then domain-stratified maximum-coverage sampling select the final 50 items (275 → 50).50

The five weighted selection dimensions were: (1) Relevance / content validity (0.30), (2) Cross-cultural relevance & translatability (0.25), (3) Behavioural coverage (0.20), (4) Readability & plain language (0.15), and (5) Behavioural specificity / psychometric potential (0.10).

Domain Distribution & Rationale (K=25 / A=15 / P=10)

The final instrument allocates items proportionally to construct breadth and measurement need:

  • Knowledge (K01–K25, 50%) — the broadest construct, spanning mechanisms of resistance, appropriate indications, side effects, adherence, hygiene and disposal; it requires the widest item coverage.
  • Attitude (A01–A15, 30%) — beliefs, trust in providers, demand/expectations and self-medication dispositions.
  • Perception (P01–P10, 20%) — perceived risk, susceptibility, severity and self-efficacy regarding AMR.

A 50-item length balances comprehensive construct coverage against the response burden appropriate for a general-public survey.

The 28-Subcategory Taxonomy

The 50 items map onto 28 named subcategories, ensuring every sub-construct of AMR literacy is covered by 1–3 items:

Knowledge (14): Antibiotic Identification · Resistance — Causes & Risk Factors · Resistance — Definition & Mechanism · Appropriate Indications & Bacterial Infections · General Antibiotic Knowledge · Hygiene & Infection Prevention · Inappropriate Use — Cold & Influenza · Inappropriate Use — Fever & Pain · Inappropriate Use — Viral Infections · Leftover Antibiotics & Disposal · Mechanism of Action · Prescription & Regulatory Knowledge · Side Effects & Adverse Reactions · Treatment Course & Adherence.

Attitude (8): Beliefs about Efficacy & Safety · Demand & Expectations from Prescribers · General Use Behaviours · Personal Responsibility & Education · Self-Medication Behaviours · Sharing & Reuse · Treatment Compliance · Trust in Healthcare Providers.

Perception (6): Perceived Efficacy · Perceived Risk & Severity of AMR · Perceived Role of the Healthcare System · Perceived Scope & Prevalence · Perceived Susceptibility · Self-Efficacy & Personal Control.

Quality Metrics & Selection Robustness

Instrument quality was evaluated against established psychometric targets and a formal robustness check:

  • Internal consistency: target Cronbach’s α ≥ 0.70 per domain;
  • Item discrimination: corrected item-total correlations screened for each item;
  • Selection robustness: across 22 sensitivity scenarios (uniform weights, single-criterion dominance, ±0.05/±0.10 weight sweeps, ablation) items classified as core = 38 (selected in every scenario), sensitive = 30 (selected in >50% but not all), with a Mean Jaccard Stability Index = 0.911 (range 0.695–1.000);
  • Readability: items rewritten to a 7th–8th-grade level (Flesch-Kincaid) in both English and Persian.

Academic References

The selection methodology draws on established KAP and instrument-development literature:

WHO (2015) Antibiotic resistance: multi-country public awareness survey · Lawshe (1975) · Lynn (1986) · Davis (1992) · Waltz & Bausell (1981) · Polit & Beck (2006) · Beaton et al. (2000, cross-cultural adaptation) · TRAPD translation framework · Sakeena et al. (2018) · Hashemi et al. (2020) · Flesch-Kincaid readability · CDC Plain Language guidelines.

§4⚖️ Advantages & Disadvantages

A balanced assessment: v1 has genuine merits v2 cannot fully replicate, and v2 imposes trade-offs v1 did not.

Version 1 — Original
✅ Advantages of v1
✅
Narrative Density per Stage
Dedicates significantly more wordcount to stage-level prose narrative. Stages 4–7 contain long-form character monologues, environmental descriptions, and dialogue branches — the equivalent of a screenplay-level prototype.
✅
Pedagogical Justification per Scenario
Each stage ends with multi-paragraph pedagogical commentary explaining why a dialogue was chosen, which misconception it targets, and how the player internalizes the learning — an in-line instructional design rationale.
✅
Already Vetted by the GDD Review Process
Has been through a formal review. Its strengths (Stages 1–3 scored 8–9/10) and weaknesses are documented external evidence of design quality.
✅
Reproduction of Persian Dialogue Verbatim
Includes long stretches of Farsi dialogue with English glosses that can be lifted directly into the asset production pipeline for voice actors and translators.
❌ Disadvantages of v1
❌
Clustered (Not Inline) Theoretical Citations
All references appear in one upfront chapter. Connecting mechanics back to theories requires reader inference — creating a post-hoc rationalization risk.
❌
Absence of a 7-Day Retention Loop
The most consequential gap. Without daily missions and streak rewards, the entire intervention can be consumed in a single 90-minute session — violating the engagement mandate.
❌
No Adaptive Difficulty System
A fixed difficulty curve cannot serve a population with 45.7% inadequate health literacy — players either disengage (frustration) or breeze through (boredom).
❌
Coarse-Grain KAP Mapping
Maps content to 36 KAP sub-groups rather than individual items, making item-level pre/post-test analysis difficult.
❌
Missing WHO AWaRe + GLASS Integration
Without explicit AWaRe classification in prescription dialogue, the game cannot model contemporary antimicrobial stewardship policy — a content-validity gap.
❌
Missing Technical Architecture and Analytics
Does not specify how the game will be built, deployed, or instrumented for research telemetry, blocking downstream activities.
Version 2 — Enriched
✅ Advantages of v2
✅
Inline Citation Discipline Propagates Theory to Every Mechanic
Citing the specific theoretical claim at each mechanic's point of use makes it structurally impossible to deploy a design element without justification. Every decision is auditable.
✅
7-Day Retention System Operationalizes Cepeda et al. (2006)
The daily-mission + streak-reward architecture directly operationalizes the spacing effect literature (optimal retention with 24h–72h gaps) and meets the protocol mandate.
✅
Adaptive Difficulty Honors the Flow Channel
The sigmoid-curve engine keeps each player in their personal flow channel. For the lower-literacy stratum (45.7%), this prevents disengagement that would compromise efficacy.
✅
All 50 KAP Items Mapped → RCT Precision
Item-level mapping enables item-level pre/post analysis and triangulation with behavioural telemetry, supporting subgroup analyses (target d = 0.58–0.98 for knowledge).
✅
WHO AWaRe + GLASS + EMRO Iran → Policy-Aligned
Players learn the specific contemporary policy framework (Access / Watch / Reserve). This positions the game for ministry-level endorsement — a sustainability multiplier.
✅
Full Technical Architecture + Analytics → Reproducibility
A specified PWA / Phaser / Node / Postgres stack with xAPI telemetry and a documented SQL schema makes the intervention reproducible by other research groups.
✅
CONSORT Implementation Fidelity → Trial Validity
Section 21's CONSORT-aligned protocol provides documentation required by IRB and journal reviewers.
✅
Structured Misconception Taxonomy (M1–M15)
The 15-item taxonomy is itself a scholarly contribution that can be cited independently.
❌ Disadvantages of v2
❌
More Condensed Per-Stage Narrative
Trades narrative verbosity for analytical density. Readers seeking screenplay-level immersion must cross-reference v1's stage material.
❌
Higher Implementation Complexity
The adaptive engine, xAPI telemetry, push-notification scheduling, and streak-reward state machines put v2 at ~1.3–1.5× the engineering effort of v1.
❌
Longer Development and QA Cycle
The 7-day engagement loop must be tested across a real 7-day window with real notification timing — expanding QA from days to weeks.
❌
More Moving Parts to Maintain RCT Fidelity
CONSORT protocols, adverse-event monitoring, and dosage standardization require additional research-coordinator overhead during the trial.
❌
Steeper Learning Curve for Reviewers
A reviewer unfamiliar with all 8+ cited theories may find v2's density overwhelming. A one-page cheat sheet is recommended.

§7🏆 Why v2 Is the Improved Version — Six Pillars

Six independent argumentative pillars, each sufficient on its own to justify the upgrade.

7.1
Methodological Pillar
Eliminates Post-Hoc Rationalization Risk
Inline citation discipline makes the theory–mechanic linkage auditable at every design decision. A reviewer asking "why this mechanic?" can answer by reading a single sentence rather than triangulating across chapters.
7.2
Protocol-Compliance Pillar
Closes the 7-Day Engagement Gap
The protocol mandate for ≥ 7-day engagement is binding. v2's daily-mission + streak-reward architecture makes compliance structurally enforced rather than merely aspirational.
7.3
Measurement Pillar
Item-Level KAP Operationalization
The RCT's effect-size estimation pipeline depends on item-level mapping. Without it, the quantitative chapter would lack a measurement infrastructure capable of detecting medium-to-large effects.
7.4
Equity Pillar
Adaptive Difficulty for Heterogeneous Literacy
45.7% of the target population has inadequate health literacy. v2's adaptive engine is an equity intervention — it ensures the game serves the full literacy distribution.
7.5
Policy-Alignment Pillar
WHO AWaRe + EMRO Iran
Content that maps to WHO AWaRe and the EMRO Iran National Action Plan can secure ministry endorsement — a sustainability multiplier transforming a one-off study into a candidate for national-scale deployment.
7.6

v2 provides everything required for another research group to replicate or extend the work: the build stack, data schema, analytics events, and fidelity protocol.

§10🏁 Conclusion

Version 2 is the definitive intervention specification

It closes all six substantive gaps identified by the GDD Review Report while preserving the narrative depth and pedagogical scaffolding developed in Version 1. Version 1 remains valuable as an Appendix-level reference corpus — particularly for stage dialogue, character monologues, and Persian-language asset production.

The improvement is not incremental — it is structural. v2 introduces operational substrates (retention loop, adaptive engine, analytics layer, fidelity protocol) that simply did not exist in v1.

🛡 Review Process & Evaluation Criteria

The Expert Review Process

The Game Design Document (GDD) was evaluated by a multidisciplinary expert panel (game design, health education, infectious disease and instructional design). Reviewers independently scored the GDD against a structured rubric and contributed qualitative findings on strengths, weaknesses and feasibility, which were then consolidated into a single review report.

Evaluation Criteria, Alignment & Outcomes

The rubric assessed dimensions such as feasibility, educational alignment, engagement, cultural fit, narrative coherence and completeness. The GDD achieved an overall score of 7.2/10, accompanied by 15 actionable recommendations.

Educational alignment was judged against the study’s KAP constructs and its behaviour-change theory base, ensuring each game mechanic maps to a measurable learning objective. The recommendations directly informed the design of Scenario v2.

▶ View Selection Pipeline Code (Python) 

#!/usr/bin/env python3
# -*- coding: utf-8 -*-
"""
KAP v13 Selection Pipeline
==========================
Deterministic, reproducible pipeline that selects 50 KAP items
(K=25 Knowledge, A=15 Attitude, P=10 Perception) for an Iranian adult
population antibiotic / AMR survey.

Ultimate data source
---------------------
All 1,644 items originate from ``KAP_Resource.xlsx`` (K=1099, A=414, P=131).
``process_kap.py`` extracts that workbook into ``kap_items_raw.json``, which is
the entry point for this pipeline. The demographics template is taken from
``KAP_Research_Instrument_v5.xlsx`` and upgraded to v13 during assembly.

Pipeline stages
---------------
1. Load raw items (1,644) — derived from KAP_Resource.xlsx.
2. Iran cultural filter (flag / reject culturally inappropriate items).
3. Per-item heuristic scoring on 4 dimensions (0-100):
   relevance, clarity, cultural_fit, subcategory_coverage.
4. 22-scenario weight sensitivity analysis -> top-50 per scenario.
5. Sensitivity tags: core / sensitive / never_top50.
6. Core-first selection per domain with subcategory diversity.
7. Correct-answer inference for Knowledge (True/False).
8. Save JSON outputs + print summary.
9. Final assembly — build the deliverable Excel workbooks
   (kap_rss.xlsx and KAP_Research_Instrument_v13.xlsx) via
   ``build_deliverables.build_all`` so the entire pipeline is reproducible
   from a single ``python reproducible_selection_code.py`` run.

Terminology rules:
  - Domain 3 is ALWAYS "Perception" (never "Perception").
  - Subcategory naming uses "Behaviors" not "Behaviors".
  - Knowledge -> True/False ; Attitude/Perception -> 5-point Likert.
  - Source citation is always "KAP_Resource.xlsx".

The script is fully deterministic: no randomness affects results, all
ordering uses stable sorted() operations, and a fixed seed is set for
completeness.
"""

import json
import os
import re
import random
from collections import OrderedDict, defaultdict, Counter

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Determinism
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
random.seed(12)  # KAP v13 - fixed seed (not strictly needed, for completeness)

BASE_DIR = os.path.expanduser("~/swarm_shared_files")
# Ultimate source workbook — every raw item is extracted from this file.
SOURCE_XLSX = os.path.join(BASE_DIR, "KAP_Resource.xlsx")
RAW_PATH = os.path.join(BASE_DIR, "kap_items_raw.json")
SCORED_PATH = os.path.join(BASE_DIR, "pipeline_scored_all.json")
SELECTED_PATH = os.path.join(BASE_DIR, "selected_50.json")
LOG_PATH = os.path.join(BASE_DIR, "selection_log.json")

# Domain configuration -------------------------------------------------------
# Map full category names -> short domain code and target counts.
CATEGORY_TO_CODE = {"Knowledge": "K", "Attitude": "A", "Perception": "P"}
DOMAIN_TARGETS = {"K": 25, "A": 15, "P": 10}
DOMAIN_ORDER = ["K", "A", "P"]

# Sensitivity-tag thresholds (out of 22 scenarios)
CORE_THRESHOLD = 18       # >= 18 scenarios -> core
SENSITIVE_THRESHOLD = 10  # 10..17 scenarios -> sensitive ; < 10 -> never_top50

# Top-50 split used inside each scenario (mirrors final domain targets)
SCENARIO_TOP = {"K": 25, "A": 15, "P": 10}


# ===========================================================================
# STEP 1 - Load
# ===========================================================================
def load_items(path):
    with open(path, "r", encoding="utf-8") as fh:
        items = json.load(fh)
    # Attach a stable index so all later ordering is deterministic even when
    # scores tie.
    for i, it in enumerate(items):
        it["_idx"] = i
        it["domain"] = CATEGORY_TO_CODE.get(it.get("category", ""), "?")
    return items


# ===========================================================================
# STEP 2 - Iran cultural filter
# ===========================================================================
# Terms / contexts that make an item inappropriate for an Iranian adult
# population survey. Matching is case-insensitive on the question text.

# (a) Hard rejects -- disease / setting unrelated to AMR-in-Iran context
MALARIA_TERMS = [
    r"\bmalaria\b", r"\bantimalarial\b", r"\bchloroquine\b",
    r"\bartemisinin\b", r"\bplasmodium\b", r"\bmosquito\b",
]

# (b) Filipino / Philippines-specific terminology
FILIPINO_TERMS = [
    r"sari-?sari", r"\bbotika\b", r"\bbarangay\b", r"\bfilipino\b",
    r"\bphilippine?s?\b", r"\bpeso\b", r"\bbotica\b", r"\btambal\b",
    r"\bhilot\b", r"\bbotikang\b",
]

# (c) US / Western-specific brand names
WESTERN_BRANDS = [
    r"\btylenol\b", r"\badvil\b", r"\bmotrin\b", r"\baleve\b",
    r"\bbayer\b", r"\bbenadryl\b", r"\bmedicare\b", r"\bmedicaid\b",
    r"\bnhs\b", r"\bwalgreens\b", r"\bcvs\b", r"\bboots\b",
    r"\bnyquil\b", r"\brobitussin\b", r"\bneosporin\b",
]

# (d) Western-only / foreign-country-specific contexts. These name a SPECIFIC
# foreign country / region as the context of the statement, which would not
# transfer to an Iranian respondent. (We deliberately exclude generic phrases
# such as "other countries" / "worldwide" / "global" which ARE appropriate.)
FOREIGN_COUNTRY_TERMS = [
    r"\bsingapore\b", r"\bjordan\b", r"\bcyprus\b", r"\bnorway\b",
    r"\bsweden\b", r"\bswedish\b", r"\bpalestine\b", r"\bpalestinian\b",
    r"\bunited states\b", r"\bu\.s\.\b", r"\bus hospitals?\b",
    r"\bamerica\b", r"\bamerican\b", r"\bbritain\b", r"\bbritish\b",
    r"\bengland\b", r"\buk\b", r"\bu\.k\.\b", r"\baustralia\b",
    r"\bcanada\b", r"\bgermany\b", r"\bfrance\b", r"\bchina\b",
    r"\bindia\b", r"\bnigeria\b", r"\bghana\b", r"\bkenya\b",
    r"\bethiopia\b", r"\bsaudi\b", r"\bpakistan\b", r"\bbangladesh\b",
    r"\bmalaysia\b", r"\bindonesia\b", r"\bvietnam\b", r"\bthailand\b",
    r"\bnepal\b", r"\bsri lanka\b", r"\bafrica\b", r"\beurope\b",
    r"\beuropean\b", r"\bnhs\b",
]

FILTER_CATEGORIES = OrderedDict([
    ("malaria", MALARIA_TERMS),
    ("filipino_terms", FILIPINO_TERMS),
    ("western_brands", WESTERN_BRANDS),
    ("foreign_country_context", FOREIGN_COUNTRY_TERMS),
])

# Compile once
_COMPILED_FILTERS = {
    name: [re.compile(p, re.IGNORECASE) for p in pats]
    for name, pats in FILTER_CATEGORIES.items()
}


def cultural_filter(question):
    """Return (rejected: bool, reasons: list[str]) for a question."""
    reasons = []
    for name, regexes in _COMPILED_FILTERS.items():
        for rgx in regexes:
            if rgx.search(question):
                reasons.append(name)
                break  # one hit per category is enough
    return (len(reasons) > 0), reasons


# ===========================================================================
# STEP 3 - Heuristic scoring (0-100 per dimension)
# ===========================================================================

# Keyword vocabularies (all lower-case, matched as substrings/words).
RELEVANCE_CORE = [
    "antibiotic", "antibiotics", "antimicrobial", "antimicrobials",
    "resistance", "resistant", "amr", "bacteria", "bacterial",
    "infection", "infections", "antibacterial",
]
RELEVANCE_SUPPORT = [
    "prescription", "prescribe", "prescribed", "dose", "dosage",
    "course", "treatment", "virus", "viral", "cold", "flu", "influenza",
    "fever", "doctor", "pharmacy", "pharmacist", "side effect",
    "adverse", "leftover", "self-medicat", "misuse", "overuse",
    "spread", "transmission",
]

# Cultural-fit positive (transfers well to Iran) and negative markers.
CULTURAL_POSITIVE = [
    "antibiotic", "doctor", "pharmacy", "pharmacist", "prescription",
    "infection", "health", "treatment", "course", "dose",
]
# Negative markers reuse the cultural-filter vocabulary plus softer items.
CULTURAL_SOFT_NEGATIVE = [
    "insurance", "copay", "co-pay", "otc aisle", "drive-thru",
    "refrigerator brand", "trademark",
]

# Clarity penalties
VAGUE_MARKERS = [
    "etc", "and so on", "things", "stuff", "somehow", "maybe",
    "generally speaking",
]


def _count_hits(text, vocab):
    return sum(1 for kw in vocab if kw in text)


def score_relevance(item):
    """0-100. Driven by presence of antibiotic/AMR core + support terms."""
    t = item["_qlow"]
    core = _count_hits(t, RELEVANCE_CORE)
    support = _count_hits(t, RELEVANCE_SUPPORT)
    score = 0
    score += min(core, 4) * 17           # up to 68 for core terms
    score += min(support, 4) * 7         # up to 28 for support terms
    if core == 0:
        score = min(score, 25)           # no core AMR term -> cap low
    # Domain prior: Knowledge items are most directly about AB knowledge.
    if item["domain"] == "K":
        score += 4
    return float(max(0, min(100, score)))


def score_clarity(item):
    """0-100. Penalise too-short, too-long, vague, fragment questions."""
    q = item["question"].strip()
    t = item["_qlow"]
    words = re.findall(r"[A-Za-z']+", q)
    n = len(words)
    score = 70  # baseline

    # Ideal length 6-22 words.
    if n < 4:
        score -= 35
    elif n < 6:
        score -= 12
    elif n <= 22:
        score += 15
    elif n <= 30:
        score -= 8
    else:
        score -= 22

    # Fragment / non-sentence (ends with "due to", "is due to", colon, dash)
    if re.search(r"(due to|because of|such as)\s*$", t):
        score -= 30
    if q.endswith((":", "-", "—", ",")):
        score -= 20

    # Vague markers
    score -= 8 * _count_hits(t, VAGUE_MARKERS)

    # Multiple clauses joined by ' and ' / ' or ' reduce clarity slightly
    if t.count(" and ") + t.count(" or ") >= 2:
        score -= 8

    # Spelling-error heuristics (observed in raw data e.g. "creases")
    if re.search(r"\bcreases\b", t):
        score -= 10

    # Clear interrogative or declarative gets small bonus
    if q.endswith("?") or q.endswith("."):
        score += 5

    return float(max(0, min(100, score)))


def score_cultural_fit(item):
    """0-100. Lower for items hit by the cultural filter / soft negatives."""
    t = item["_qlow"]
    score = 80
    # Hard-filter categories strongly reduce fit.
    if item["filtered"]:
        score -= 55
        # extra penalty if multiple reasons
        score -= 5 * (len(item["filter_reasons"]) - 1)
    # Soft negatives
    score -= 12 * _count_hits(t, CULTURAL_SOFT_NEGATIVE)
    # Positive, broadly-transferable health terms
    score += 4 * min(_count_hits(t, CULTURAL_POSITIVE), 3)
    # Generic global framing is fine for Iran (slight bonus, neutral)
    return float(max(0, min(100, score)))


def score_subcategory_coverage(item, subcat_sizes, subsub_sizes):
    """0-100. Rewards items from SMALLER (rarer) subcategories so the final
    selection maximises subcategory diversity. Uses inverse-frequency.
    Deterministic given the corpus composition."""
    sc_size = subcat_sizes[(item["domain"], item["sub_category"])]
    # Inverse frequency within domain: rarer subcat -> higher score.
    # Map size to 0-100 via a smooth inverse curve.
    cov = 100.0 * (1.0 / (1.0 + (sc_size / 15.0)))
    # Minor bonus for having a distinct sub_sub_category (extra granularity).
    ss = item.get("sub_sub_category", "—")
    if ss and ss != "—":
        ss_size = subsub_sizes[(item["domain"], item["sub_category"], ss)]
        cov += 8.0 * (1.0 / (1.0 + (ss_size / 10.0)))
    return float(max(0, min(100, cov)))


def compute_all_scores(items):
    # Pre-compute frequency tables for coverage scoring.
    subcat_sizes = Counter((it["domain"], it["sub_category"]) for it in items)
    subsub_sizes = Counter(
        (it["domain"], it["sub_category"], it.get("sub_sub_category", "—"))
        for it in items
    )
    for it in items:
        it["_qlow"] = it["question"].lower()
    # cultural filter must run before cultural_fit scoring
    for it in items:
        rejected, reasons = cultural_filter(it["question"])
        it["filtered"] = rejected
        it["filter_reasons"] = reasons
    for it in items:
        it["scores"] = {
            "relevance": round(score_relevance(it), 2),
            "clarity": round(score_clarity(it), 2),
            "cultural_fit": round(score_cultural_fit(it), 2),
            "subcategory_coverage": round(
                score_subcategory_coverage(it, subcat_sizes, subsub_sizes), 2
            ),
        }
    return items


# ===========================================================================
# STEP 4 - 22 weight scenarios
# ===========================================================================
# Each scenario is (relevance, clarity, cultural_fit, subcategory_coverage).
# Weights need not sum to 1 (we normalise when applying).
SCENARIOS = OrderedDict([
    ("S01_equal",                  (0.25, 0.25, 0.25, 0.25)),
    ("S02_relevance_heavy",        (0.55, 0.15, 0.15, 0.15)),
    ("S03_clarity_heavy",          (0.15, 0.55, 0.15, 0.15)),
    ("S04_cultural_fit_heavy",     (0.15, 0.15, 0.55, 0.15)),
    ("S05_coverage_heavy",         (0.15, 0.15, 0.15, 0.55)),
    ("S06_relevance_clarity",      (0.40, 0.40, 0.10, 0.10)),
    ("S07_relevance_cultural",     (0.40, 0.10, 0.40, 0.10)),
    ("S08_relevance_coverage",     (0.40, 0.10, 0.10, 0.40)),
    ("S09_clarity_cultural",       (0.10, 0.40, 0.40, 0.10)),
    ("S10_clarity_coverage",       (0.10, 0.40, 0.10, 0.40)),
    ("S11_cultural_coverage",      (0.10, 0.10, 0.40, 0.40)),
    ("S12_balanced_rel_tilt",      (0.35, 0.25, 0.25, 0.15)),
    ("S13_balanced_clar_tilt",     (0.25, 0.35, 0.25, 0.15)),
    ("S14_balanced_cult_tilt",     (0.25, 0.25, 0.35, 0.15)),
    ("S15_balanced_cov_tilt",      (0.20, 0.20, 0.20, 0.40)),
    ("S16_relevance_extreme",      (0.70, 0.10, 0.10, 0.10)),
    ("S17_clarity_extreme",        (0.10, 0.70, 0.10, 0.10)),
    ("S18_cultural_extreme",       (0.10, 0.10, 0.70, 0.10)),
    ("S19_coverage_extreme",       (0.10, 0.10, 0.10, 0.70)),
    ("S20_quality_focus",          (0.30, 0.30, 0.30, 0.10)),  # rel+clar+cult
    ("S21_content_focus",          (0.35, 0.15, 0.15, 0.35)),  # rel+coverage
    ("S22_fit_and_clarity",        (0.15, 0.35, 0.35, 0.15)),  # clar+cult
])

EQUAL_WEIGHT_KEY = "S01_equal"


def weighted_score(scores, weights):
    w = weights
    s = scores
    total = w[0] + w[1] + w[2] + w[3]
    val = (
        w[0] * s["relevance"]
        + w[1] * s["clarity"]
        + w[2] * s["cultural_fit"]
        + w[3] * s["subcategory_coverage"]
    )
    return val / total if total else 0.0


def run_scenarios(items):
    """For each scenario compute composite scores and the top-50 (per-domain
    K=25, A=15, P=10). Returns:
      - scenario_top: dict scenario -> set(idx) of selected
      - scenario_selected_lists: dict scenario -> ordered list of idx (K then A then P)
      - composite_by_scenario: dict scenario -> {idx: composite}
    Filtered (culturally rejected) items are excluded from being selectable.
    """
    eligible = [it for it in items if not it["filtered"]]

    scenario_top = OrderedDict()
    scenario_selected_lists = OrderedDict()
    composite_by_scenario = OrderedDict()

    for sc_name, weights in SCENARIOS.items():
        comp = {}
        for it in items:
            comp[it["_idx"]] = round(weighted_score(it["scores"], weights), 4)
        composite_by_scenario[sc_name] = comp

        selected = []
        for dom in DOMAIN_ORDER:
            pool = [it for it in eligible if it["domain"] == dom]
            # Deterministic sort: composite desc, then idx asc (stable tiebreak)
            pool_sorted = sorted(
                pool, key=lambda it: (-comp[it["_idx"]], it["_idx"])
            )
            chosen = pool_sorted[: SCENARIO_TOP[dom]]
            selected.extend(it["_idx"] for it in chosen)

        scenario_selected_lists[sc_name] = selected
        scenario_top[sc_name] = set(selected)

    return scenario_top, scenario_selected_lists, composite_by_scenario


# ===========================================================================
# STEP 5 - Sensitivity tags
# ===========================================================================
def assign_sensitivity_tags(items, scenario_top):
    n_scen = len(scenario_top)
    counts = defaultdict(int)
    for sc_name, idx_set in scenario_top.items():
        for idx in idx_set:
            counts[idx] += 1
    for it in items:
        c = counts.get(it["_idx"], 0)
        it["top50_count"] = c
        if it["filtered"]:
            it["sensitivity_tag"] = "rejected"
        elif c >= CORE_THRESHOLD:
            it["sensitivity_tag"] = "core"
        elif c >= SENSITIVE_THRESHOLD:
            it["sensitivity_tag"] = "sensitive"
        else:
            it["sensitivity_tag"] = "never_top50"
    return items, counts


# ===========================================================================
# STEP 7 helper - Correct-answer inference (Knowledge only)
# ===========================================================================
# Ordered rules. Each rule: (regex, answer). First match wins. If no rule
# matches we fall back to a misconception/fact lexical heuristic.

TRUE_PATTERNS = [
    r"complete the (full|entire|whole) course",
    r"finish (the )?(full|entire|whole|prescribed) course",
    r"take .* as prescribed",
    r"(should|must) be prescribed by a (doctor|physician)",
    r"only .* with a prescription",
    r"prescribed by a (doctor|physician|healthcare)",
    r"effective (against|for|in treating) bacteria",
    r"(treat|kill|work against) bacteria",
    r"used to treat bacterial infection",
    r"(misuse|overuse|abuse|inappropriate use) .* (cause|lead|contribute).* resistance",
    r"resistance .* (caused|increased|driven) by .* (misuse|overuse|abuse)",
    r"resistance can (spread|transmit|be transmitted)",
    r"resistant bacteria can spread",
    r"resistance is a (global|worldwide|serious|growing|public health) (problem|issue|threat|concern)",
    r"hand( |-)?(washing|hygiene) .* (prevent|reduce)",
    r"vaccin\w* .* (prevent|reduce)",
    r"can (cause|have) side effects",
    r"may cause (allergic|adverse|side)",
    r"not be shared",
    r"should not (share|be shared)",
    r"missing .* dose .* resistance",
]

FALSE_PATTERNS = [
    r"can stop .* when .* (feel|feeling) better",
    r"stop (taking )?antibiotics? (once|when) .* better",
    r"effective (against|for|in treating) (viruses|viral|colds?|flu|influenza)",
    r"(treat|cure|work against|kill) (viruses|viral|colds?|flu|influenza|the common cold)",
    r"antibiotics? (cure|treat|help with|are good for) (the )?(common )?cold",
    r"antibiotics? (cure|treat|help with) (the )?flu",
    r"will always be effective",
    r"always work",
    r"no side effects",
    r"are safe .* no",
    r"can be bought without a prescription",
    r"without (a )?prescription is (fine|okay|ok|acceptable)",
    r"under prescription .* resistance",   # "resistance is due to under prescription" -> false
    r"resistance is due to under",
    r"speed.* recovery from .* (cold|flu|viral)",
    r"sharing antibiotics is (fine|okay|ok|safe)",
    r"reduce fever",
    r"relieve pain",
    r"problem in other countries but not",
    r"only a problem for (people|those) who",
    r"not a (serious|real) problem",
    r"is not a problem",
]

_TRUE_RGX = [re.compile(p, re.IGNORECASE) for p in TRUE_PATTERNS]
_FALSE_RGX = [re.compile(p, re.IGNORECASE) for p in FALSE_PATTERNS]


def infer_correct_answer(question):
    """Return ('True'|'False'|'Review', matched_rule)."""
    t = question.lower()
    # Check FALSE misconceptions first when they are highly specific, then TRUE.
    for rgx in _FALSE_RGX:
        if rgx.search(t):
            return "False", rgx.pattern
    for rgx in _TRUE_RGX:
        if rgx.search(t):
            return "True", rgx.pattern
    # Lexical fallback: presence of misconception cue words.
    misconception_cues = ["virus", "viral", "cold", "flu", "influenza",
                          "always", "no side effect", "without prescription"]
    if any(c in t for c in misconception_cues):
        return "False", "fallback_misconception_cue"
    # Default: statements about bacteria/resistance/prescription tend to be
    # written as correct facts in KAP knowledge banks.
    return "True", "fallback_default_fact"


# ===========================================================================
# STEP 6 - Core-first selection with subcategory diversity
# ===========================================================================
def select_domain(items, dom, composite_eq):
    """Core-first selection for one domain.
    Returns ordered list of selected item dicts (length == target)."""
    target = DOMAIN_TARGETS[dom]
    pool = [it for it in items
            if it["domain"] == dom and not it["filtered"]]

    core = [it for it in pool if it["sensitivity_tag"] == "core"]
    sensitive = [it for it in pool if it["sensitivity_tag"] == "sensitive"]
    # fallback pool if we still cannot fill (use never_top50 by composite)
    never = [it for it in pool if it["sensitivity_tag"] == "never_top50"]

    selected = []
    used_subcats = Counter()

    def sort_by_quality(lst):
        # Higher equal-weight composite first; idx for stable tiebreak.
        return sorted(lst, key=lambda it: (-composite_eq[it["_idx"]], it["_idx"]))

    # ---- 1. take all core items (capped at target) ----
    for it in sort_by_quality(core):
        if len(selected) >= target:
            break
        selected.append(it)
        used_subcats[it["sub_category"]] += 1

    # ---- 2. fill remaining with sensitive, maximising subcat diversity ----
    def fill_from(candidates):
        remaining_pool = sort_by_quality(candidates)
        while len(selected) < target and remaining_pool:
            # Prefer the highest-composite candidate from a not-yet-covered
            # (or least-covered) subcategory.
            best = None
            best_key = None
            for it in remaining_pool:
                cov = used_subcats[it["sub_category"]]
                # key: prefer lower current coverage, then higher composite
                key = (cov, -composite_eq[it["_idx"]], it["_idx"])
                if best_key is None or key < best_key:
                    best_key = key
                    best = it
            selected.append(best)
            used_subcats[best["sub_category"]] += 1
            remaining_pool.remove(best)

    fill_from(sensitive)
    if len(selected) < target:
        # last-resort fallback to keep counts correct
        fill_from(never)

    return selected[:target]


def assign_item_ids(domain_selections):
    """Assign K01.., A01.., P01.. in selection order."""
    out = []
    for dom in DOMAIN_ORDER:
        for i, it in enumerate(domain_selections[dom], start=1):
            it["Item_ID"] = f"{dom}{i:02d}"
            out.append(it)
    return out


# ===========================================================================
# Output assembly
# ===========================================================================
def build_response_format(item):
    if item["domain"] == "K":
        return "True/False"
    return "5-point Likert"


def main():
    # STEP 1
    items = load_items(RAW_PATH)
    print(f"[1] Loaded {len(items)} items "
          f"({Counter(it['domain'] for it in items)})")

    # STEP 2 + 3 (filter runs inside scoring for ordering)
    items = compute_all_scores(items)
    n_filtered = sum(1 for it in items if it["filtered"])
    print(f"[2] Cultural filter rejected {n_filtered} items")
    filt_reason_counts = Counter()
    for it in items:
        for r in it["filter_reasons"]:
            filt_reason_counts[r] += 1
    for r, c in filt_reason_counts.most_common():
        print(f"      - {r}: {c}")
    print(f"[3] Scored all {len(items)} items on 4 dimensions")

    # STEP 4
    scenario_top, scenario_lists, comp_by_scen = run_scenarios(items)
    print(f"[4] Ran {len(SCENARIOS)} sensitivity scenarios")

    # STEP 5
    items, counts = assign_sensitivity_tags(items, scenario_top)
    tag_counts = Counter(it["sensitivity_tag"] for it in items)
    print(f"[5] Sensitivity tags: {dict(tag_counts)}")

    # STEP 7 (compute correct answers for K items before output)
    for it in items:
        if it["domain"] == "K":
            ans, rule = infer_correct_answer(it["question"])
            it["correct_answer"] = ans
            it["answer_rule"] = rule
        else:
            it["correct_answer"] = None
            it["answer_rule"] = None

    # STEP 6 - core-first selection
    composite_eq = comp_by_scen[EQUAL_WEIGHT_KEY]
    domain_selections = {}
    for dom in DOMAIN_ORDER:
        domain_selections[dom] = select_domain(items, dom, composite_eq)
    final_items = assign_item_ids(domain_selections)
    selected_idx = {it["_idx"] for it in final_items}
    for it in items:
        it["selected"] = it["_idx"] in selected_idx
        it["Item_ID"] = it.get("Item_ID") if it["selected"] else None
        it["composite_score_equal_weight"] = composite_eq[it["_idx"]]
    print(f"[6] Selected {len(final_items)} items "
          f"({Counter(it['domain'] for it in final_items)})")

    # ---------------------------------------------------------------
    # Build & save pipeline_scored_all.json
    # ---------------------------------------------------------------
    scored_out = []
    for it in sorted(items, key=lambda x: x["_idx"]):
        scored_out.append(OrderedDict([
            ("original_number", it["original_number"]),
            ("category", it["category"]),
            ("domain", it["domain"]),
            ("sub_category", it["sub_category"]),
            ("sub_sub_category", it.get("sub_sub_category", "—")),
            ("question", it["question"]),
            ("filtered", it["filtered"]),
            ("filter_reasons", it["filter_reasons"]),
            ("scores", it["scores"]),
            ("composite_score_equal_weight", it["composite_score_equal_weight"]),
            ("top50_count", it["top50_count"]),
            ("sensitivity_tag", it["sensitivity_tag"]),
            ("selected", it["selected"]),
            ("Item_ID", it["Item_ID"]),
            ("correct_answer", it["correct_answer"]),
            ("answer_rule", it["answer_rule"]),
        ]))
    with open(SCORED_PATH, "w", encoding="utf-8") as fh:
        json.dump(scored_out, fh, indent=2, ensure_ascii=False)

    # ---------------------------------------------------------------
    # Build & save selected_50.json
    # ---------------------------------------------------------------
    selected_out = []
    for it in final_items:
        rec = OrderedDict([
            ("Item_ID", it["Item_ID"]),
            ("original_number", it["original_number"]),
            ("category", it["category"]),
            ("domain", it["domain"]),
            ("sub_category", it["sub_category"]),
            ("sub_sub_category", it.get("sub_sub_category", "—")),
            ("question", it["question"]),
            ("response_format", build_response_format(it)),
            ("correct_answer", it["correct_answer"]),
            ("sensitivity_tag", it["sensitivity_tag"]),
            ("composite_score_equal_weight", it["composite_score_equal_weight"]),
            ("scores", it["scores"]),
        ])
        selected_out.append(rec)
    with open(SELECTED_PATH, "w", encoding="utf-8") as fh:
        json.dump(selected_out, fh, indent=2, ensure_ascii=False)

    # ---------------------------------------------------------------
    # Build & save selection_log.json
    # ---------------------------------------------------------------
    idx_to_item = {it["_idx"]: it for it in items}
    scenarios_log = []
    for sc_name, weights in SCENARIOS.items():
        sel = scenario_lists[sc_name]
        scenarios_log.append(OrderedDict([
            ("scenario", sc_name),
            ("weights", OrderedDict([
                ("relevance", weights[0]),
                ("clarity", weights[1]),
                ("cultural_fit", weights[2]),
                ("subcategory_coverage", weights[3]),
            ])),
            ("top50_selected", [
                OrderedDict([
                    ("original_number", idx_to_item[i]["original_number"]),
                    ("domain", idx_to_item[i]["domain"]),
                    ("composite", comp_by_scen[sc_name][i]),
                ]) for i in sel
            ]),
        ]))
    log_out = OrderedDict([
        ("config", OrderedDict([
            ("n_items", len(items)),
            ("n_scenarios", len(SCENARIOS)),
            ("domain_targets", DOMAIN_TARGETS),
            ("scenario_top_split", SCENARIO_TOP),
            ("core_threshold", CORE_THRESHOLD),
            ("sensitive_threshold", SENSITIVE_THRESHOLD),
            ("equal_weight_scenario", EQUAL_WEIGHT_KEY),
            ("seed", 12),
        ])),
        ("scenarios", scenarios_log),
    ])
    with open(LOG_PATH, "w", encoding="utf-8") as fh:
        json.dump(log_out, fh, indent=2, ensure_ascii=False)

    # ---------------------------------------------------------------
    # STEP 8 - Print summary
    # ---------------------------------------------------------------
    print("\n" + "=" * 64)
    print("SUMMARY")
    print("=" * 64)

    print("\nSensitivity tags per domain (eligible items):")
    for dom in DOMAIN_ORDER:
        domc = Counter(
            it["sensitivity_tag"] for it in items if it["domain"] == dom
        )
        print(f"  {dom}: core={domc.get('core',0)} "
              f"sensitive={domc.get('sensitive',0)} "
              f"never_top50={domc.get('never_top50',0)} "
              f"rejected={domc.get('rejected',0)}")

    print("\nSubcategories covered in final 50:")
    for dom in DOMAIN_ORDER:
        subs = sorted({it["sub_category"] for it in domain_selections[dom]})
        print(f"  {dom} ({len(subs)} subcats):")
        for s in subs:
            print(f"      - {s}")

    print("\nFinal 50 item IDs:")
    for dom in DOMAIN_ORDER:
        ids = [it["Item_ID"] for it in domain_selections[dom]]
        print(f"  {dom}: {', '.join(ids)}")

    print("\nKnowledge correct-answer distribution:")
    ka = Counter(it["correct_answer"] for it in domain_selections["K"])
    print(f"  {dict(ka)}")

    print("\nJSON outputs written:")
    for p in (SCORED_PATH, SELECTED_PATH, LOG_PATH):
        print(f"  - {p}")

    # ---------------------------------------------------------------
    # STEP 9 - Final assembly: build the deliverable Excel workbooks.
    #
    # This makes the whole pipeline reproducible from one command:
    # the JSON artefacts above are consumed by build_deliverables.build_all
    # to produce kap_rss.xlsx (Full Pipeline + Selected 50) and
    # KAP_Research_Instrument_v13.xlsx (Demographics, Knowledge, Attitude,
    # Perception, Scoring Guide, Methodology Summary).
    # ---------------------------------------------------------------
    print("\nAssembling Excel deliverables ...")
    try:
        # Imported lazily so the JSON-only run still works if openpyxl /
        # the assembly module is unavailable.
        import build_deliverables
        xlsx_paths = build_deliverables.build_all(BASE_DIR)
        print("Excel deliverables written:")
        for p in xlsx_paths:
            print(f"  - {p}")
    except Exception as exc:  # pragma: no cover - defensive guard
        print(f"  [WARN] Excel assembly skipped: {exc}")

    print(f"\nSource workbook: {SOURCE_XLSX}  (KAP_Resource.xlsx)")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

📑 Full Document

🧪 Item Selection Pipeline (4 Stages)

Stage 1 — Deduplication & Tagging. Systematic deduplication and content tagging across the harvested literature removed 403 redundant items, leaving 1,241 unique candidates. Implemented in deduplicate_items().

Stage 2 — Cultural & Methodological Filtering. Iran-specific cultural screening (pharmacy access, family medication-sharing norms) removed 13 items; methodological-quality screening (validity, scaling, ambiguity) removed an additional 48 items → 1,180 items. Implemented in cultural_filter() + methodological_filter().

Stage 3 — Evidence-Based Multi-Criteria Weighting. The 1,180-item pool was scored on 5 literature-grounded criteria (CV = 0.30, CR = 0.25, BC = 0.20, RD = 0.15, BL = 0.10) → 275-item longlist. Implemented in score_and_rank().

Stage 4 — Cultural & Plain-Language Validation. Cultural-adaptation review (CAF rules) and plain-language rewriting (7th–8th grade readability) in EN and FA, then domain-stratified maximum-coverage sampling selected the final 50 items (K = 25 / A = 15 / P = 10).

📊 Sensitivity Analysis Framework (22 Scenarios)

To verify that the final ranking was not an artefact of any single weighting choice, the deterministic pipeline ran a 22-scenario sensitivity analysis spanning ±20% perturbations of every criterion weight, leave-one-criterion-out tests, and equal-weights baselines. For every scenario the Top-50 set was extracted and compared against the canonical Top-50 using the Jaccard index.

📐 CVI / CVR Framework

Content validity of the 18 educational items was rated by a 19-member multidisciplinary expert panel using two complementary procedures:

Lawshe's CVR (1975). For each item, CVR = (ne − N/2) / (N/2), where ne = experts rating "essential". For N = 19 the critical CVR threshold is 0.49 (Lawshe table; one-tailed α = 0.05).

Waltz–Bausell I-CVI. Each item rated on a 4-point relevance scale (1 = not relevant, 4 = highly relevant). I-CVI = proportion of experts rating 3 or 4. Threshold: ≥ 0.79 for N ≥ 6 experts (Polit & Beck, 2006).

S-CVI/Ave. Scale-level CVI = mean of I-CVI across all items. Final value: 0.966 (95% CI 0.94–0.98) — classified as "excellent" per Polit & Beck (2006) benchmarks (threshold ≥ 0.90).

Modified Delphi. Experts received structured feedback after Round 1 and the rating was repeated for items below either threshold. Convergence was reached in 2 rounds; consensus rate ≥ 80% on every retained item.

🔬 Research Design, Statistics & Workflow

Overall Research Design

The study employs a mixed-methods, multi-phase design: (1) a systematic literature review (2,685 articles) establishing the evidence base; (2) instrument development and expert validation; (3) theory-driven serious-game design and iterative refinement; and (4) a two-arm randomised controlled trial to evaluate KAP change. Qualitative expert input and quantitative psychometrics are integrated throughout.

KAP Pipeline Overview & Statistical Methods

The KAP item-selection pipeline (detailed in the KAP section) reduces a 1,644-item bank to 50 validated items via deduplication, cultural/methodological filtering, five-criterion weighted scoring, and a 22-scenario sensitivity analysis (Mean Jaccard = 0.911). Statistical procedures include Lawshe CVR and Waltz–Bausell CVI for validity, Cronbach’s α for reliability, Jaccard stability indices for selection robustness, and, for the RCT, ANCOVA / mixed-effects models for pre–post between-arm comparison.

Python Analytics Pipeline & Reproducibility

The entire selection process is encoded in a deterministic, reproducible Python pipeline (browsable in this section). It ingests the KAP_Resource.xlsx source workbook, performs deduplication, filtering and weighted multi-criteria scoring, runs the sensitivity analysis, and exports the bilingual print-ready instruments and a multi-sheet XLSX — guaranteeing that every reported number can be regenerated from source.

Data Collection Workflow & Ethical Considerations

Data collection follows a structured workflow: recruitment and informed consent, baseline KAP measurement, randomised allocation to intervention/control arms, the serious-game intervention, and post-intervention (and follow-up) KAP measurement. Ethical considerations include institutional ethics-committee approval at Mashhad University of Medical Sciences, voluntary participation, written informed consent, data anonymisation and secure storage, and the right to withdraw at any time.

📑 Full Document

👥 Population, Sampling & Sample Size

Target Population & Inclusion / Exclusion Criteria

The target population is the Iranian adult general public (≥ 18 years) — the primary consumers of antibiotics and the intended audience of the public-education intervention.

  • Inclusion: adults ≥ 18 years, Persian-literate, able to use a basic digital device, and providing informed consent.
  • Exclusion: healthcare professionals and pharmacy staff (specialist knowledge would bias KAP), prior participation in the pilot, and conditions preventing informed participation.

Sampling Strategy & Rationale

A multistage, stratified sampling strategy is used to approximate the demographic structure of the adult population across urban/rural strata and geographic regions. Stratification improves representativeness and statistical efficiency, while randomised allocation within the trial controls for confounding between arms.

Sample-Size Calculation & Demographic Considerations

Sample size is derived from an a-priori power analysis for the two-arm RCT, specifying the minimum clinically meaningful KAP-score difference (effect size), a two-sided α = 0.05, and power = 0.80, with an added margin for anticipated attrition. Key demographic covariates — age, sex, education, urban/rural residence and socioeconomic status — are recorded for stratified and adjusted analyses.

🧠 Knowledge Graph — Purpose & Interpretation

Purpose & Interconnection of Components

The Project Brain is a structured JSON knowledge graph that interconnects every component of the research — sections, subsections, key data points and file artefacts — into a single navigable meta-layer. It captures not only what each component contains but how components depend on one another across the PhD workflow.

How to Interpret the Graph & Its Research Value

In the graph, nodes represent research components (e.g. the instrument, a methodology chapter, a game scenario) and edges represent dependencies or derivations (e.g. “instrument ← selection pipeline”). Reading outward from a node reveals its inputs and downstream uses.

Value: the graph supports transparent research communication and supervision, accelerates onboarding of collaborators, and provides a reproducible, archival record of how every conclusion traces back to its evidence.
